highlights: Algiers balances Europe and the Sahel

frictionVectors.title: European gas leverage
frictionVectors.details: Algeria retains strong control over hydrocarbons, but European demand, pricing, and energy-transition policies constrain export strategy and investment choices.

frictionVectors.title: Sahel security spillover
frictionVectors.details: Instability along Algeria's southern borders pressures surveillance, trade corridors, and diplomatic relations with neighboring military-led governments.

highlights: Lobito Corridor becomes a strategic prize

frictionVectors.title: Lobito Corridor competition
frictionVectors.details: The United States, European partners, and China are competing for influence over the corridor linking Angolan infrastructure to critical-mineral supply chains in the Copperbelt.

frictionVectors.title: Hydrocarbon and debt dependence
frictionVectors.details: Declining oil output, foreign-operated fields, and debt-linked infrastructure financing limit Luanda's ability to convert resource wealth into durable sovereign leverage.

highlights: Northern security is the strategic test

frictionVectors.title: Niger pipeline and border strain
frictionVectors.details: Tensions with Niger have disrupted trade and complicated the operation of the Niger-Benin oil-export corridor, exposing Benin's infrastructure to regional political shocks.

frictionVectors.title: Sahel militant expansion
frictionVectors.details: Jihadist violence near the northern frontier is increasing pressure on roads, parks, and border communities while drawing greater reliance on external security assistance.

highlights: Diversification is now a sovereignty priority

frictionVectors.title: Debswana market dependence
frictionVectors.details: Botswana retains substantial influence through its diamond partnership with De Beers, but weak global diamond demand can reduce fiscal space and negotiating leverage.

frictionVectors.title: Critical-minerals infrastructure gap
frictionVectors.details: Efforts to develop copper, nickel, and other minerals face transport, power, and water constraints that could increase dependence on foreign capital and processing networks.

frictionVectors.title: Russian security alignment
frictionVectors.details: Ouagadougou's closer security relationship with Russia expands room to reject Western conditionality but creates new dependence on external military and political support.

frictionVectors.title: Gold-sector control versus insurgency
frictionVectors.details: The government is seeking greater state oversight and local processing of gold, while jihadist activity threatens mines, transport routes, and the formalization of artisanal production.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign Control of Critical Minerals
frictionVectors.details: Nickel and rare-earth development remains heavily dependent on foreign capital, technology, and export channels, limiting Burundi's bargaining power over downstream value.

frictionVectors.title: Rwanda Border and Security Friction
frictionVectors.details: Mutual accusations over armed groups and border insecurity continue to constrain regional trade and encourage reliance on external diplomatic and security partners.

frictionVectors.title: External Dependence in Ports and Energy
frictionVectors.details: Port modernization, fuel supply, and renewable-energy expansion rely substantially on foreign finance and contractors, creating long-term exposure to creditor and investor priorities.

frictionVectors.title: Atlantic Security Competition
frictionVectors.details: Cabo Verde's location draws growing interest from European, North American, and other maritime-security partners, requiring careful management of basing and surveillance arrangements.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign Influence over Energy and Mining
frictionVectors.details: Hydrocarbon production and emerging mining projects remain dependent on external firms and financing, while opaque contracting limits domestic capture of resource rents.

frictionVectors.title: Critical Trade Corridors Under Strain
frictionVectors.details: The Douala-Central African Republic corridor and northern routes face insecurity, congestion, and political risk, increasing dependence on foreign logistics and security support.

frictionVectors.title: Security-for-Resources Dependence
frictionVectors.details: The government's reliance on Russian-linked security personnel has strengthened regime survival but has also increased outside influence over mining access and strategic decision-making.

frictionVectors.title: Mining Corridors Escape State Oversight
frictionVectors.details: Gold and diamond production remains concentrated in informal and conflict-affected zones, with armed groups, foreign traders, and neighboring transit networks capturing much of the value.

frictionVectors.title: External Security Realignment
frictionVectors.details: The drawdown of France's long-standing military role has widened room for new foreign security and political partnerships while leaving Chad exposed to capability gaps and regional pressure.

frictionVectors.title: Oil Infrastructure and Revenue Concentration
frictionVectors.details: State finances remain highly dependent on oil exports and externally financed infrastructure, limiting economic sovereignty and making revenue vulnerable to production and pipeline disruptions.

frictionVectors.title: France–Mayotte Sovereignty Dispute
frictionVectors.details: Moroni continues to reject French control of Mayotte, while the island’s migration controls and security presence constrain bilateral relations.

frictionVectors.title: Dependence on External Capital
frictionVectors.details: Limited domestic fiscal capacity leaves ports, energy, and transport projects dependent on foreign donors, Gulf partners, and diaspora remittances.

frictionVectors.title: Cobalt and Copper Leverage
frictionVectors.details: Chinese firms retain major influence across copper and cobalt processing, while Kinshasa seeks greater domestic refining, contract renegotiation, and supply-chain control.

frictionVectors.title: Eastern Conflict and Resource Smuggling
frictionVectors.details: Armed groups and cross-border networks continue to threaten mining zones in the east, with Rwanda-linked tensions and illicit mineral flows undermining state sovereignty.

highlights: China remains a key infrastructure partner

frictionVectors.title: Hydrocarbon Dependence
frictionVectors.details: State revenues remain highly exposed to offshore oil production and volatile prices, limiting diversification and bargaining power over foreign operators.

frictionVectors.title: Debt-Linked Infrastructure Influence
frictionVectors.details: Chinese financing and construction remain important for roads and public works, creating long-term dependence despite efforts to restructure debt and widen partnerships.

frictionVectors.title: Cocoa Processing and Pricing Power
frictionVectors.details: The government is pushing local processing and stronger farmer protections, but multinational traders still retain significant influence over financing, logistics, and global pricing.

frictionVectors.title: Port and Energy Partnerships
frictionVectors.details: Foreign operators remain central to Abidjan’s port, power, and transport expansion, though diversified investment is improving the state’s negotiating position.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign Military Base Dependence
frictionVectors.details: U.S., Chinese, French, Japanese, and other military facilities provide essential revenues and security but constrain Djibouti’s strategic autonomy amid Red Sea tensions.

frictionVectors.title: Port and Corridor Competition
frictionVectors.details: Djibouti’s logistics dominance faces pressure from Ethiopian diversification and rival regional corridors, while debt and foreign ownership complicate control of critical infrastructure.

frictionVectors.title: External financing and asset sales
frictionVectors.details: IMF-linked reforms and Gulf-backed investment provide liquidity but increase foreign influence over strategic land, ports, and state assets. Debt-service pressure limits Cairo's room to reject externally preferred projects.

frictionVectors.title: Nile water security
frictionVectors.details: The unresolved GERD dispute with Ethiopia remains Egypt's most serious strategic resource concern. Cairo continues to seek binding operating guarantees while balancing diplomacy against the risk of regional escalation.

frictionVectors.title: Hydrocarbon dependence
frictionVectors.details: Falling mature-field production and limited economic diversification weaken the state's bargaining position with foreign energy firms and lenders. LNG and gas monetization projects offer partial relief but require substantial external capital and technology.

frictionVectors.title: Port and infrastructure exposure
frictionVectors.details: Malabo's infrastructure network remains closely tied to Chinese construction finance and broader external contracting relationships. Underused capacity and opaque debt terms constrain sovereign control over long-term infrastructure planning.

frictionVectors.title: Mining-sector dependence
frictionVectors.details: Gold, copper, and zinc projects provide vital foreign exchange but leave Eritrea dependent on outside capital, equipment, and commodity markets. Limited transparency and sanctions-related risks complicate efforts to convert mineral wealth into broad sovereign development.

frictionVectors.title: Red Sea and Ethiopia rivalry
frictionVectors.details: Eritrea's ports and coastline are strategically valuable as Ethiopia seeks reliable maritime access. Rivalry with Addis Ababa, combined with shifting Gulf and Middle Eastern security interests, keeps infrastructure and sovereignty risks elevated.

frictionVectors.title: South African economic exposure
frictionVectors.details: Eswatini's customs receipts, supply chains, and electricity links remain heavily dependent on South Africa. This provides stability but restricts independent control over trade, energy, and fiscal policy.

frictionVectors.title: Investment and governance risk
frictionVectors.details: Political tensions and governance concerns reduce access to diversified Western and multilateral investment. The resulting reliance on regional partners and selected foreign investors limits the country's leverage over infrastructure finance.

frictionVectors.title: Nile diplomacy
frictionVectors.details: The GERD expands Ethiopia's control over domestic power generation and export potential, but its operation remains a major source of friction with Egypt and Sudan. Disagreements over drought-year releases and data sharing continue to carry escalation risk.

frictionVectors.title: Infrastructure and debt dependence
frictionVectors.details: Rail, telecom, energy, and industrial projects remain reliant on Chinese, Gulf, Turkish, and multilateral finance and expertise. Debt restructuring, foreign-exchange shortages, and conflict-related damage reduce Addis Ababa's ability to set wholly independent infrastructure priorities.

highlights: Military transition tightens state control over extractives
Manganese and oil remain exposed to external capital

frictionVectors.title: French commercial influence
frictionVectors.details: The post-coup authorities are renegotiating longstanding French-linked economic relationships while seeking broader partnerships. This expands policy space but risks investor uncertainty.

frictionVectors.title: Manganese logistics dependence
frictionVectors.details: Gabon relies heavily on foreign operators, financing, and transport infrastructure to monetize manganese and iron ore. Disruptions on rail and port corridors could quickly reduce state revenues.

highlights: Senegal remains the indispensable security and trade partner
Banjul seeks port-led sovereignty without fiscal room

frictionVectors.title: Senegalese corridor dependence
frictionVectors.details: The Gambia depends on access through Senegal for much of its regional commerce and security environment. This gives Dakar structural leverage over transport, border management, and energy connectivity.

frictionVectors.title: Port modernization pressure
frictionVectors.details: Foreign-backed upgrades around Banjul could improve customs and trade capacity, but may also lock the country into externally directed infrastructure and concession terms.

highlights: Accra pushes local value capture in mining and energy

frictionVectors.title: Gold-sector leakage
frictionVectors.details: Illegal mining, foreign trading networks, and environmental damage continue to weaken Ghana's control over gold value chains. Formalization efforts face resistance from entrenched domestic and external interests.

frictionVectors.title: IMF and creditor constraints
frictionVectors.details: Fiscal consolidation and debt-restructuring requirements narrow the government's room to subsidize energy, build infrastructure, or renegotiate resource contracts. External financing remains central to macroeconomic stability.

highlights: Junta centralizes mining decisions and political authority

frictionVectors.title: Simandou consortium competition
frictionVectors.details: The iron-ore project concentrates leverage among Chinese, Western, and regional commercial actors. Rail and port infrastructure could transform state revenue, but financing and offtake terms may embed long-term external dependence.

frictionVectors.title: Bauxite-sector concentration
frictionVectors.details: Guinea remains heavily dependent on foreign-controlled bauxite production, logistics, and refining markets. The authorities' push for local processing risks confrontation with operators and trading partners.

highlights: Political fragility weakens control over strategic assets
Cashew and port networks remain externally dominated

frictionVectors.title: Bissau port vulnerability
frictionVectors.details: The capital's port and customs system are vulnerable to political capture, weak oversight, and foreign commercial pressure. Limited state capacity makes infrastructure concessions difficult to monitor or enforce.

frictionVectors.title: Cashew-chain dependence
frictionVectors.details: Cashew exports provide essential foreign exchange but leave producers exposed to foreign buyers, seasonal price swings, and limited domestic processing. Senegalese and other regional networks retain significant influence over trade routes.

frictionVectors.title: Chinese Infrastructure Exposure
frictionVectors.details: Kenya is renegotiating the fiscal and strategic costs of Chinese-backed transport projects, especially around the Standard Gauge Railway and Mombasa logistics corridor. Nairobi is diversifying partners but remains exposed to refinancing and concession pressures.

frictionVectors.title: Lamu Corridor Contestation
frictionVectors.details: The Lamu Port-South Sudan-Ethiopia Transport corridor offers strategic autonomy but faces insecurity, local land disputes, and uncertain regional demand. Gulf, Chinese, and Western commercial interests are competing for influence over future logistics and energy infrastructure.

frictionVectors.title: Highlands Water Dependency
frictionVectors.details: Lesotho's water exports to South Africa provide vital revenue but bind national infrastructure and fiscal planning to Pretoria. The Highlands Water Project creates leverage for Lesotho while limiting its independent bargaining power.

frictionVectors.title: Political and Security Vulnerability
frictionVectors.details: Chronic coalition instability and economic dependence increase the influence of South African institutions and external donors. Security-sector tensions can quickly become a regional issue because Lesotho is geographically enclosed by South Africa.

frictionVectors.title: Mineral Concession Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Iron ore and other mining projects are central to Liberia's growth strategy, but foreign operators retain substantial control over capital, transport, and export chains. The government is under pressure to improve local value capture, royalties, and labor standards.

frictionVectors.title: Buchanan and Rail Corridor Competition
frictionVectors.details: Control of rail links and port infrastructure gives mining investors outsized influence over Liberia's trade geography. Concession renewals and infrastructure financing could draw stronger competition among Western, Chinese, and regional commercial actors.

frictionVectors.title: Hydrocarbon Governance Fragmentation
frictionVectors.details: Competing political and armed centers continue to use oil facilities, export approvals, and budget access as instruments of power. Foreign energy companies and neighboring states must navigate a system where formal sovereignty does not guarantee operational control.

frictionVectors.title: External Military Footprint
frictionVectors.details: Turkish, Russian-linked, Egyptian, Emirati, and other external networks retain influence through security partnerships, contractors, and political channels. Their presence constrains national decision-making and raises the risk that infrastructure disruptions become proxy confrontations.

frictionVectors.title: Mining-Contract Sovereignty
frictionVectors.details: Nickel, cobalt, ilmenite, and other mineral projects attract major foreign capital but leave Madagascar exposed to price cycles, tax disputes, and limited domestic processing. Antananarivo is seeking better terms while remaining dependent on external technology and infrastructure.

frictionVectors.title: Power and Logistics Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Unreliable electricity, weak roads, and constrained ports increase the bargaining power of foreign developers and lenders. Chinese, Gulf, European, and regional actors are competing for influence over transport, energy, and agricultural corridors.

frictionVectors.title: Mining Concession Leverage
frictionVectors.details: Uranium, rare-earth and graphite projects are drawing foreign capital, but limited domestic processing capacity risks leaving Malawi dependent on external firms and export markets.

frictionVectors.title: Energy and Fuel Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Electricity shortages, fuel-import exposure and weak transport infrastructure constrain economic sovereignty and increase sensitivity to external financing.

highlights: Junta tightens control over gold sector

frictionVectors.title: Gold Contract Confrontation
frictionVectors.details: Authorities are seeking greater state participation and revenue from industrial gold mines, creating sustained friction with foreign operators and investors.

frictionVectors.title: Security Corridor Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Reliance on Russian-linked security assistance has increased strategic autonomy from Western partners while exposing Mali to sanctions, financing constraints and escalating insurgent threats.

highlights: Gas exports enter a strategic phase

frictionVectors.title: GTA Gas Governance
frictionVectors.details: The Greater Tortue Ahmeyim project can strengthen state revenues, but dependence on foreign operators and cross-border coordination with Senegal limits immediate domestic control.

frictionVectors.title: Iron Ore and Green Hydrogen Pressure
frictionVectors.details: Foreign-backed iron-ore and proposed green-hydrogen projects promise infrastructure gains, but land, water, export-corridor and local-value concerns remain significant.

frictionVectors.title: Chagos Settlement Implementation
frictionVectors.details: The long-running sovereignty and security arrangements surrounding the Chagos Archipelago remain sensitive, especially regarding the future operation of Diego Garcia.

frictionVectors.title: Port and Digital Infrastructure Competition
frictionVectors.details: Mauritius is balancing Indian, Chinese, Gulf and Western interest in ports, logistics and telecommunications while protecting its position as a trusted financial hub.

frictionVectors.title: Western Sahara Resource Legitimacy
frictionVectors.details: Phosphate, fisheries and renewable-energy activity in Western Sahara continue to generate legal and diplomatic friction despite expanding international support for Morocco's autonomy proposal.

frictionVectors.title: External Supply-Chain Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Automotive, aerospace and renewable industries are strengthening industrial sovereignty, but remain exposed to European markets, imported energy technology and foreign capital.

highlights: Cabo Delgado security still constrains LNG sovereignty

frictionVectors.title: LNG project security and foreign control
frictionVectors.details: Insurgency and weak state reach in Cabo Delgado continue to give foreign energy firms and security partners substantial leverage over project timelines and operating conditions.

frictionVectors.title: Resource revenue and local-content tensions
frictionVectors.details: Public expectations for gas benefits remain high while debt pressures, limited domestic processing, and uneven local employment fuel concerns over extractive arrangements.

highlights: Green hydrogen ambitions attract strategic capital

frictionVectors.title: Foreign stakes in uranium, oil, and critical minerals
frictionVectors.details: International investors are competing for uranium, offshore hydrocarbons, and emerging critical-mineral assets, testing Namibia's regulatory capacity and demands for domestic value addition.

frictionVectors.title: Green-hydrogen infrastructure dependence
frictionVectors.details: Large hydrogen and renewable projects depend on external finance, technology, and export corridors, creating potential sovereignty risks if local ownership and water safeguards lag.

highlights: Security and export isolation constrain revenue

frictionVectors.title: Uranium and mining relations with foreign operators
frictionVectors.details: The junta's effort to renegotiate or reclaim greater control over uranium and other minerals has intensified friction with established foreign companies and external partners.

frictionVectors.title: Pipeline and border-security disruption
frictionVectors.details: Insurgent violence, sanctions exposure, and strained regional relations threaten oil-export infrastructure and raise the cost of maintaining reliable routes to international markets.

frictionVectors.title: Refinery sovereignty versus imported supply
frictionVectors.details: New domestic refining capacity can reduce dependence on imported petroleum products, but feedstock constraints, pricing disputes, and infrastructure bottlenecks limit strategic autonomy.

frictionVectors.title: Oil theft and foreign-investment friction
frictionVectors.details: Pipeline vandalism, crude theft, and regulatory uncertainty continue to weaken state capture of petroleum value while complicating cooperation with international oil companies.

highlights: Mineral governance is tied to regional conflict

frictionVectors.title: Eastern Congo minerals and diplomatic pressure
frictionVectors.details: Rwanda's security posture and alleged links to mineral flows from eastern Democratic Republic of the Congo continue to generate regional and international scrutiny over resource sovereignty.

frictionVectors.title: Critical-mineral processing dependency
frictionVectors.details: The country seeks to expand domestic processing and logistics, but financing, technology, and export-market access remain heavily dependent on external partners.

highlights: Gulf of Guinea energy hopes remain speculative
Small-state diplomacy balances Europe and China

frictionVectors.title: Offshore hydrocarbons uncertainty
frictionVectors.details: Exploration in disputed or underdeveloped offshore blocks offers potential leverage but has yet to produce dependable state revenue. Limited administrative and maritime capacity increases reliance on external operators.

frictionVectors.title: External financing dependence
frictionVectors.details: Infrastructure and budget support remain heavily dependent on Portugal, multilateral lenders, and other partners, constraining policy autonomy without creating a single dominant foreign patron.

highlights: New oil and gas revenue sharpens sovereignty agenda

frictionVectors.title: Hydrocarbon contract renegotiation
frictionVectors.details: The government is seeking greater transparency and national benefit from offshore oil and gas projects involving international firms. Aggressive renegotiation could improve control but risks investment delays, arbitration, or production disruptions.

frictionVectors.title: Strategic infrastructure dependence
frictionVectors.details: Ports, railways, energy systems, and digital infrastructure attract competing French, Chinese, Gulf, and Turkish interests. Dakar is attempting diversification while managing debt and the political sensitivity of foreign concessions.

highlights: Blue economy remains the sovereignty cornerstone

frictionVectors.title: Foreign control of fisheries value chains
frictionVectors.details: Seychelles retains strong regulatory capacity, but foreign fleets and processing interests remain central to tuna revenues. Monitoring access, licensing, and sustainability is vital to prevent value leakage.

frictionVectors.title: Indian Ocean strategic competition
frictionVectors.details: India, China, European states, and Gulf actors compete for maritime access, surveillance, and port influence. Victoria benefits from this competition but must avoid becoming overdependent on any security provider.

highlights: Mining drives growth but limits domestic value capture
Freetown seeks leverage over strategic concessions

frictionVectors.title: Iron ore and rutile dependence
frictionVectors.details: Large-scale mining generates export earnings but leaves the state exposed to commodity cycles, foreign capital, and limited local processing. Contract terms, taxation, and community benefits remain central sovereignty concerns.

frictionVectors.title: Port and corridor competition
frictionVectors.details: Foreign-backed port, logistics, and mining-corridor projects could improve connectivity while locking in long-term concessions. Debt, transparency, and local-content safeguards will determine whether infrastructure expands or narrows national control.

highlights: Federal authority expands unevenly beyond Mogadishu
Offshore resources remain a sovereignty test

frictionVectors.title: Resource and revenue-sharing disputes
frictionVectors.details: Offshore oil licensing and broader resource governance are contested between the federal government and member states. Weak institutional trust and constitutional disputes create openings for foreign firms to exploit fragmented authority.

frictionVectors.title: Competing port and security patrons
frictionVectors.details: Turkey, the United Arab Emirates, Qatar, and other partners support ports, security forces, and logistics networks with competing strategic interests. External assistance strengthens capacity but can deepen federal-regional rivalry and dilute unified maritime control.

frictionVectors.title: Strategic-minerals competition
frictionVectors.details: South Africa is seeking more domestic processing and beneficiation of platinum-group metals, manganese and other critical minerals. Competition among China, the United States, the European Union and Gulf investors limits Pretoria's room to dictate terms.

frictionVectors.title: Eskom and freight constraints
frictionVectors.details: Unreliable electricity and underperforming rail and port networks continue to reduce export capacity and weaken state control over mining logistics. Private-sector participation is expanding, but implementation remains politically sensitive.

frictionVectors.title: Pipeline dependence on Sudan
frictionVectors.details: South Sudan's oil exports depend on infrastructure crossing war-affected Sudan, exposing revenues and production to sabotage, outages and bargaining pressure from Khartoum and armed actors.

frictionVectors.title: External control of petroleum flows
frictionVectors.details: Foreign operators, trading arrangements and security intermediaries remain central to the petroleum sector, while weak institutions and elite competition limit transparent national control over oil income.

highlights: Gold and port access drive rivalry

frictionVectors.title: Gold-sector externalization
frictionVectors.details: Gold production and smuggling networks finance competing armed coalitions and attract external commercial and political sponsors. The state has little effective control over major extraction and export channels.

frictionVectors.title: Red Sea infrastructure contest
frictionVectors.details: Port Sudan and associated transport corridors are strategic targets for regional powers seeking military access, trade leverage and influence over Sudan's future resource exports.

highlights: LNG and corridor projects advance cautiously

frictionVectors.title: LNG bargaining and financing
frictionVectors.details: Negotiations over large offshore gas development continue to balance national revenue, domestic energy needs and investor protections. Delays reflect Dar es Salaam's effort to secure stronger local benefits without deterring capital.

frictionVectors.title: Ports and strategic corridors
frictionVectors.details: Foreign-backed port, railway and logistics projects are expanding Tanzania's regional leverage but generate concerns about debt exposure, concession terms and long-term control of critical infrastructure.

highlights: Lomé remains a regional trade hub

frictionVectors.title: Port and logistics influence
frictionVectors.details: The Port of Lomé is central to Togo's economic strategy and attracts Gulf, Chinese, European and regional commercial interests. Dependence on external capital and operators constrains full national control over logistics infrastructure.

frictionVectors.title: Phosphate-sector governance
frictionVectors.details: Phosphate resources remain strategically important, but production and downstream processing are limited by financing, technology and governance challenges. Foreign partnerships are necessary yet reduce the state's ability to capture the full value chain.

frictionVectors.title: EU migration and financing pressure
frictionVectors.details: European funding and market access remain tied to migration management, limiting Tunisian policy autonomy. Domestic resistance to externally driven economic conditions complicates cooperation.

frictionVectors.title: Energy import dependence
frictionVectors.details: Tunisia remains vulnerable to imported energy costs and grid constraints while pursuing renewable projects and deeper electricity links with Europe. Phosphate-sector weakness further limits export earnings.

frictionVectors.title: EACOP sovereignty and financing
frictionVectors.details: The oil pipeline and associated fields promise revenue but leave Uganda exposed to foreign operators, lenders, litigation, and environmental scrutiny. Export dependence through Tanzania constrains strategic flexibility.

frictionVectors.title: Critical infrastructure concentration
frictionVectors.details: Chinese and Gulf-linked capital remains important in transport, energy, and construction. Debt service and project terms raise concerns about long-term fiscal and strategic dependence.

highlights: Debt reset improves room to maneuver

frictionVectors.title: Copper-sector external influence
frictionVectors.details: Zambia is attracting competing Chinese, Western, and Gulf investment in copper and critical minerals. The government is seeking greater processing, tax, and ownership benefits while avoiding renewed investor flight.

frictionVectors.title: Debt and infrastructure conditionality
frictionVectors.details: Debt restructuring has eased immediate pressure but leaves fiscal policy shaped by creditors and multilateral lenders. Rail, power, and logistics bottlenecks continue to limit domestic control over mineral value chains.

frictionVectors.title: Mineral competition and value capture
frictionVectors.details: Zimbabwe is using export controls and beneficiation demands to retain more value from lithium, platinum, and other minerals. Chinese dominance in mining and processing remains central, while Western firms seek alternative access.

frictionVectors.title: Sanctions and financial isolation
frictionVectors.details: Sanctions exposure, restricted capital access, and exchange-rate instability raise the cost of infrastructure and mineral development. Dependence on external buyers and informal payment channels weakens sovereign bargaining power.
